title: Self Joins and Many Tables
summary: Join three tables in one query, join a table to itself, and build every combination.
intro: Real questions often span more than two tables, or link a table to its own rows. This lesson chains joins across four tables, joins a table to itself with two aliases, and builds every combination with CROSS JOIN.

steps.title: Three tables in one query
steps.body:
This part uses a small shop. `customers (id, name)` holds Ana, Ben, and Cleo. `products (id, name, price)` holds a Notebook at 3.50, a Pen at 1.25, a Backpack at 24.00, and a Mug at 8.00. Orders and their lines live in two more tables:

```text
 id | customer_id | ordered_on
----+-------------+------------
  1 |           1 | 2025-03-01
  2 |           2 | 2025-03-02
  3 |           1 | 2025-03-05
  4 |           3 | 2025-03-07
(4 rows)

 order_id | product_id | qty
----------+------------+-----
        1 |          1 |   2
        1 |          2 |   5
        2 |          3 |   1
        3 |          2 |   3
        3 |          4 |   2
        4 |          1 |   1
        4 |          4 |   1
(7 rows)
```

An order line holds only ids, so you follow each id to its table. Every `JOIN ... ON` adds one more table, matched to a table already in the query:

```sql harness
SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, oi.qty
{{code}}
ORDER BY o.id, p.id;
```

```sql
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products AS p ON p.id = oi.product_id
```

Read the joins left to right: orders with customers, that result with order lines, and that with products. The planner may run them in any order with the same result. Each `ON` may use any alias joined before it. Give every table a short alias and name every column with it, because `name` is in both `customers` and `products` and a bare `name` fails with `column reference "name" is ambiguous`.

Plain `JOIN` drops rows with no match, at every step. A customer with no orders disappears from the result, just as in a two table join. If you keep such rows with `LEFT JOIN`, make the joins after it `LEFT JOIN` too, or a later plain `JOIN` drops them again.

example.title: Order lines in words
example.prompt: List every order line with the customer, the product, and the line total.
example.code:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, oi.qty * p.price AS line_total
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products AS p ON p.id = oi.product_id
ORDER BY o.id, p.name;
example.output:
order_id | customer | product  | line_total
----------+----------+----------+------------
        1 | Ana      | Notebook |       7.00
        1 | Ana      | Pen      |       6.25
        2 | Ben      | Backpack |      24.00
        3 | Ana      | Mug      |      16.00
        3 | Ana      | Pen      |       3.75
        4 | Cleo     | Mug      |       8.00
        4 | Cleo     | Notebook |       3.50
(7 rows)
example.explanation: Each order joins its customer through `customer_id`, then its lines through `order_id`, then each line's product through `product_id`. One row comes out per order line, and `oi.qty * p.price` mixes columns from two different tables. Sorting by order id, then product name, keeps the result stable because no order has the same product twice.

practice.title: What each customer bought
practice.prompt:
List every product each customer ordered, with the quantity and the order date.

1. Start from `customers` as `c` and join `orders` as `o`, `order_items` as `oi`, and `products` as `p`.
2. Select `c.name` as `customer`, `p.name` as `product`, `oi.qty`, and `o.ordered_on`.
3. Sort by customer name, then product name, then `o.id`.

Expected output:

```text
 customer | product  | qty | ordered_on
----------+----------+-----+------------
 Ana      | Mug      |   2 | 2025-03-05
 Ana      | Notebook |   2 | 2025-03-01
 Ana      | Pen      |   5 | 2025-03-01
 Ana      | Pen      |   3 | 2025-03-05
 Ben      | Backpack |   1 | 2025-03-02
 Cleo     | Mug      |   1 | 2025-03-07
 Cleo     | Notebook |   1 | 2025-03-07
(7 rows)
```
practice.starter:
-- TODO: join order_items and products, then show the product and qty
SELECT c.name AS customer, o.ordered_on
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY c.name, o.id;
practice.solution:
SELECT c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, oi.qty, o.ordered_on
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products AS p ON p.id = oi.product_id
ORDER BY c.name, p.name, o.id;
hints: Each new `JOIN` matches one id: orders by `customer_id`, lines by `order_id`, products by `product_id`.
Add two `JOIN` lines after the orders join: `order_items` matched on its `order_id`, then `products` matched on the line's `product_id`.
With `p` and `oi` in the query, add `p.name AS product` and `oi.qty` to the `SELECT` list and `p.name` to the `ORDER BY`.

steps.title: Joining a table to itself
steps.body:
A column can point at another row of the same table. In `staff`, `manager_id` holds the id of the person's manager, and Maya, at the top, has none:

```text
 id | name  | manager_id
----+-------+------------
  1 | Maya  |
  2 | Omar  |          1
  3 | Priya |          1
  4 | Liam  |          2
  5 | Nora  |          2
  6 | Theo  |          3
(6 rows)
```

To show the manager's name, join `staff` to itself. List the table twice with two different aliases, then treat them as two tables: `s` is the employee, `m` is the manager.

```sql harness
SELECT s.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
{{code}}
ORDER BY s.id;
```

```sql
FROM staff AS s
LEFT JOIN staff AS m ON m.id = s.manager_id
```

Each copy needs its own name, so give both an alias. Without them `staff.name` could mean either copy, and PostgreSQL refuses the query:

```text
ERROR:  table name "staff" specified more than once
```

Try `SELECT staff.name FROM staff JOIN staff ON staff.id = staff.manager_id;` in the editor to see it.

Pick the join for the question. With a plain `JOIN`, Maya drops out, because her `manager_id` is NULL and `m.id = NULL` is never true. A `LEFT JOIN` keeps her with an empty manager. To list managers and their reports instead, flip the sides: an inner join keeps only people who manage someone.

example.title: Everyone and their manager
example.prompt: List each staff member with their manager's name, keeping the person who has no manager.
example.code:
SELECT s.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM staff AS s
LEFT JOIN staff AS m ON m.id = s.manager_id
ORDER BY s.id;
example.output:
employee | manager
----------+---------
 Maya     |
 Omar     | Maya
 Priya    | Maya
 Liam     | Omar
 Nora     | Omar
 Theo     | Priya
(6 rows)
example.explanation: Each row of `s` looks for the row of `m` whose `id` equals its `manager_id`. Omar's `manager_id` is 1, so `m` is Maya. Maya's `manager_id` is NULL and matches nothing, so the `LEFT JOIN` keeps her and fills `manager` with NULL, which prints as nothing.

practice.title: Who reports to whom
practice.prompt:
List every manager with each person who reports to them.

1. Join `staff` as `m` (the manager) to `staff` as `s` (the report) on `s.manager_id = m.id`, with a plain `JOIN`.
2. Select `m.name` as `manager` and `s.name` as `report`.
3. Sort by manager name, then report name, then `s.id`.

Expected output:

```text
 manager | report
---------+--------
 Maya    | Omar
 Maya    | Priya
 Omar    | Liam
 Omar    | Nora
 Priya   | Theo
(5 rows)
```
practice.starter:
-- TODO: join staff to itself so each row pairs a manager with a report
SELECT s.name AS report
FROM staff AS s
ORDER BY s.name, s.id;
practice.solution:
SELECT m.name AS manager, s.name AS report
FROM staff AS m
JOIN staff AS s ON s.manager_id = m.id
ORDER BY m.name, s.name, s.id;

tests.output:
manager | report
---------+--------
 Maya    | Omar
 Maya    | Priya
 Omar    | Liam
 Omar    | Nora
 Priya   | Theo
(5 rows)

tests.stdin:
UPDATE staff SET manager_id = 3 WHERE id = 5;
INSERT INTO staff (id, name, manager_id) VALUES (7, 'Iris', 6), (8, 'Ezra', NULL);
tests.output:
manager | report
---------+--------
 Maya    | Omar
 Maya    | Priya
 Omar    | Liam
 Priya   | Nora
 Priya   | Theo
 Theo    | Iris
(6 rows)

hints: Write `staff` twice in the `FROM`, once as `m` and once as `s`.
The `ON` matches a report to its manager: the report's `manager_id` equals the manager's `id`.
A plain `JOIN` drops anyone who manages nobody, which is what you want here.

steps.title: Every combination with CROSS JOIN
steps.body:
`CROSS JOIN` has no `ON`: it pairs every row of one table with every row of the other. Two small tables, `sizes (size)` with S, M, and L and `colors (color)` with Black, Red, and White, give 3 × 3 = 9 rows.

```sql
SELECT size, color
FROM sizes
CROSS JOIN colors
ORDER BY size, color;
```

Use it on purpose, to build every combination: product variants, a calendar of every day for every room, a grid. The result size multiplies, so two tables of 1,000 rows give a million.

A table can cross join itself too. On `staff (id, name, manager_id)`, with Maya, Omar, Priya, Liam, Nora, and Theo, that pairs every person with every person, including themselves, and each pair shows up twice (Maya with Omar, then Omar with Maya). Keep each pair once with `WHERE a.id < b.id`: it drops the self pairs and the mirrored copies.

```sql harness
SELECT a.name AS first, b.name AS second
{{code}}
ORDER BY a.id, b.id;
```

```sql
FROM staff AS a
CROSS JOIN staff AS b
WHERE a.id < b.id
```

The old comma form `FROM sizes, colors` means the same thing. Watch for it in other people's code: a comma join that forgot its `WHERE` silently becomes a cross join.

example.title: Every shirt variant
example.prompt: List every size and color pair with a product code for each.
example.code:
SELECT size, color, 'TEE-' || size || '-' || upper(left(color, 3)) AS code
FROM sizes
CROSS JOIN colors
ORDER BY size, color;
example.output:
size | color |   code
------+-------+-----------
 L    | Black | TEE-L-BLA
 L    | Red   | TEE-L-RED
 L    | White | TEE-L-WHI
 M    | Black | TEE-M-BLA
 M    | Red   | TEE-M-RED
 M    | White | TEE-M-WHI
 S    | Black | TEE-S-BLA
 S    | Red   | TEE-S-RED
 S    | White | TEE-S-WHI
(9 rows)
example.explanation: Each of the 3 sizes meets each of the 3 colors, so 9 rows come out. The columns from both tables are in reach, so the code mixes `size` and `color`. Sizes sort as text, so L comes before M and S. The size and color pair is unique, so the order is stable.

practice.title: Pairing rota
practice.prompt:
List every pair of two different staff members, each pair once, for a pairing rota.

1. Cross join `staff` as `a` with `staff` as `b`.
2. Keep only rows where `a.id < b.id`.
3. Select `a.name` as `person_a` and `b.name` as `person_b`, sorted by `a.id`, then `b.id`.

Expected output:

```text
 person_a | person_b
----------+----------
 Maya     | Omar
 Maya     | Priya
 Maya     | Liam
 Maya     | Nora
 Maya     | Theo
 Omar     | Priya
 Omar     | Liam
 Omar     | Nora
 Omar     | Theo
 Priya    | Liam
 Priya    | Nora
 Priya    | Theo
 Liam     | Nora
 Liam     | Theo
 Nora     | Theo
(15 rows)
```

`WHERE a.id < b.id` removes both the self pairs and the mirrored pairs.

recap:
- Chain joins one at a time: each `JOIN ... ON` matches a new table to one already in the query.
- Alias every table and qualify columns with it, since names like `name` repeat across tables.
- A self join lists one table twice with two aliases, such as `staff AS s` and `staff AS m`.
- `LEFT JOIN` keeps rows with no match, like the person with no manager.
- `CROSS JOIN` pairs every row with every row, so the row count multiplies.
- On a self cross join, `WHERE a.id < b.id` keeps each pair once.
